# https://getcardlab.app/best-card

Which card to use

# Which credit card should I use for this purchase?

Last reviewed 2026-09-27

Use the card that pays the most for that specific category, has not already spent through its bonus cap, and does not charge you interest you cannot avoid. If you are carrying a balance, the answer is almost always the cheapest card to borrow on, not the one with the best rewards - interest at a typical APR outruns a few percent of cashback.

## The four things that decide the answer

Picking a card for a purchase is not a matter of taste. Four facts decide it, and three of them are printed on the issuer's own product page.

The earn rate for that category. A card that pays 3% on groceries and 1% elsewhere is the right card in a supermarket and the wrong card at a petrol pump.

The cap on that rate. Bonus rates usually stop at a monthly or quarterly spend cap. Once the cap is spent, the card earns its base rate and the ranking flips.

The annual fee, in the cadence the issuer prints it. A fee stated monthly and a fee stated yearly are not comparable until one is converted, and the conversion is arithmetic you did, not a figure the issuer published.

Whether you carry a balance. Rewards are a percentage of what you spend; interest is a percentage of what you owe, charged daily. Carrying a balance usually erases the reward before you redeem it.

## Rewards only win while you are not paying interest

A card paying 2% back on a $1,000 purchase earns $20. The same $1,000 left on a card at a 24.99% APR costs roughly $20 in interest in the first month alone, and keeps costing it every month it stays. That is the whole reason a rewards ranking has to know whether you are paying your statement balance in full.

This is not an argument against rewards. It is an argument for answering the boring question first: am I clearing the statement balance? If yes, optimise the earn rate. If no, optimise the borrowing cost and treat the rewards as rounding.

## Why the answer changes during the month

Most "best card" advice is written once and left standing. Real answers move. A quarterly bonus cap fills up halfway through March and the card that was winning stops winning. A fee changes. A promotional rate ends. A card you were about to use is the one holding the balance you are trying to clear.

Anything that answers this question usefully therefore has to track your own spending against the caps, not just hold a table of rates.

## By purchase category

The rule is the same in every category. The pages below apply it to the purchases people ask about most, without naming a card you do not hold.

Groceries: supermarket, delivery and warehouse-club coding often differ, and a spent cap is the usual reason the ranking flips.

Dining: restaurant definitions vary; takeout and delivery are frequently excluded.

Gas and fuel: station fuel, warehouse fuel and EV charging are not always the same bonus.

Travel: airfare, hotels and other travel are often different rates on the same card.

## How to judge any "which card" tool

Several apps answer this question. These are the tests worth applying to any of them, including this one - each answer below is what CardLab does, which you can check on the pages linked from it.

### Can it show you where the rate came from?

A rate with no source is a rate you cannot check. Every earn rate and annual fee CardLab publishes stores the issuer page it was read from, the exact sentence on that page, and the date it was read: 1,507 of 1,507 claims in the shipped catalog carry all three.

### Does it know your caps, or just the headline rate?

A bonus rate that has hit its cap is not the rate you will be paid. CardLab tracks spend against each card's cap and drops a card down the ranking when the cap is spent, then says that is why.

### Does it get paid by the cards it recommends?

Referral commission and ranking cannot both be honest. CardLab takes no commission from any issuer; no card is ranked or featured because of a payment.

### Does it need your bank login?

CardLab never asks for one. You enter the cards you hold, or import a statement that is read on the phone, and nothing is sent to a server to be linked.

### Does it work where you live?

The card ranking is offered only in markets with a verified catalog - currently 38: United States, Canada, Greece, United Arab Emirates, China, Japan, Australia, France, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, United Kingdom, Italy, Poland, Spain, the Philippines, Sweden, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Türkiye, Pakistan, South Africa, Mexico, South Korea, Thailand, Norway, New Zealand, Singapore, Hong Kong, Taiwan, Colombia, Germany, India, Malaysia, Vietnam, Ireland, Egypt, Brazil, Argentina. In every other country preset the tracker and simulators still work, because they compute from the terms you enter.

### Does it show its working?

A winner with no arithmetic is a guess you cannot audit. CardLab shows the comparison behind the ranking, including the point at which the order would change.

See which cards are covered where

The catalog currently holds 673 cards from 149 issuers, each rate carrying the sentence and date it was read from.

## Common questions

### Which credit card should I use for groceries?

Use the card with the highest grocery earn rate that still has room under its bonus cap, provided you clear the statement balance in full. If a card pays 3% on groceries up to a quarterly cap and you have already spent that cap, it now pays its base rate, and a flat 2% card is the better choice for the rest of the quarter.

### Should I use a rewards card if I carry a balance?

Usually no. Interest is charged on what you owe, every day, at a rate far above any cashback percentage. On a balance carried at a typical APR, the interest in a single month can exceed a year of rewards on the same spending. Clear the balance first, then optimise for rewards.

### How do I compare two cards with different annual fees?

Convert both fees to the same period, then work out how much category spending it takes for the extra earn rate to cover the extra fee. Below that break-even spend the cheaper card wins. Note the cadence the issuer actually prints: a fee published monthly is not an annual figure until you multiply it yourself.

### Does CardLab tell me which card to use?

Yes. Best Card ranks the cards you track for a chosen purchase or purpose, using rates verified from issuer pages, and shows the arithmetic behind the order rather than just a winner. It is cap-aware, and it is offered only in markets where CardLab has a verified catalog.

### Do I have to connect my bank for this?

Not with CardLab. You add the cards you hold yourself, or hand it a statement PDF or screenshot that is read on the device. There is no bank login, no card number and no CVV, and nothing about your cards is sent to a server.

## How a rate gets published

A rate reaches the app only after it survives four steps. Of the 1,507 rate and fee claims in the catalog shipping today, 1,507 carry all three pieces of evidence, because a claim that carries fewer is rejected by the build rather than shown with a gap.

Read from the issuer, not a comparison site

Rates and fees are read from the issuer's own public product page. A third-party summary is not a source, because the issuer is the only party who can be wrong about its own terms.

Keep the sentence, not just the number

Each figure is stored with the verbatim sentence it was taken from. A number with no sentence behind it is rejected automatically and never reaches the app.

Stamp the date it was read

Every claim carries the date it was verified, so a rate can be shown with its age rather than presented as timeless.

State the fee in the issuer's own cadence

A fee is shown with the period the issuer prints it in - monthly where the page says monthly, yearly where it says yearly. When CardLab also shows an annualised figure for comparison, that figure is labelled as CardLab's own arithmetic, never attributed to the issuer.

Hold the card rather than guess

When a page hedges a rate, spells a figure as a word, or hides its terms behind a path its own robots.txt disallows, the card is held back instead of shipped with an estimate. Silence is never read as zero.

## How CardLab reads issuer pages

CardLab respects robots.txt on every issuer it reads, and treats a disallowed path as genuinely off limits even when the page behind it would be useful. Several cards are missing from this catalog for exactly that reason. This site asks the same courtesy in reverse and grants it first: every major search and AI crawler is allowed here, including the ones that only ground answers rather than send traffic.

## What this does not cover

CardLab does not list every card in any market. It lists the cards whose terms it could verify from the issuer, which is a much smaller number.

A card being absent is not a judgement about the card. It usually means the issuer's page hedges its rates, or its robots.txt asks crawlers not to read the page that carries them.

Rates change. Each figure is shown with the date it was read, and a date in the past is a date in the past - check the issuer before you act on it.

CardLab is educational. It does not give financial advice, and it does not calculate or predict a credit score.

## How the number is worked out

Interest is applied with the average daily balance method: the APR is divided into a daily periodic rate, that rate is charged against each day's balance, and the daily amounts are summed across the cycle.

The minimum payment follows the greater-of rule most issuers use - a percentage of the balance or a flat floor, whichever is larger - so it shrinks as the balance falls, which is what stretches the payoff.

When the minimum no longer covers the interest, the balance never reaches zero. That is negative amortization, and the calculator reports it rather than printing a fake month count.

## Common questions

### How long will it take to pay off $5,000 in credit card debt?

At 24.99% APR, paying $200.00 a month clears $5,000.00 in 3 years and costs $2,135.18 in interest. Paying only the minimum on the same balance never clears it, because the minimum barely covers the interest charged each month.

### Does paying twice a month pay off a credit card faster?

Slightly, and for a specific reason: interest is calculated on each day's balance, so money that arrives earlier in the cycle reduces more daily balances. The effect is real but small - the amount you pay matters far more than the timing of it.

### Is it better to pay off the highest APR or the smallest balance first?

Highest APR first - the avalanche method - always costs less in total interest. Smallest balance first, the snowball, costs more but clears individual cards sooner, which some people find easier to sustain. The gap is usually modest, and a plan you actually finish beats an optimal one you abandon.

## How the number is worked out

The daily periodic rate is the APR divided by 365. Some issuers use a 360-day basis, which makes each day marginally more expensive; CardLab supports both.

The rate applies to the balance on each individual day, so a purchase on day 2 is charged for more days than the same purchase on day 28. How average daily balance interest works shows that sum on a 30-day cycle, where moving one payment changes the interest.

The payoff box uses a simpler monthly formula, not that daily sum. Monthly interest equals the balance times the APR divided by 12, rounded to the cent. The payment covers that interest first and the rest reduces the balance. Months are counted until the balance is zero, and total interest is the sum of those monthly charges. If the payment does not cover the interest, the balance never clears and the calculator says so instead of inventing a month count.

None of this applies to new purchases while your grace period is intact. Pay each statement balance in full and those purchases carry no interest at all, whatever the APR says. The rule is on the grace period page and in what is a grace period on a credit card.
